differences: Each session's state is Rust's (LiveCore, in the twin). `live.sessions` is a Map-like of views onto it: a field reads and sets Rust's, and a value read is a copy, so a change made inside it (`s.turn.active = false`, `s.prompts.push(…)`) doesn't reach Rust; set the field again. Its Maps (inflight, files, edits, mcp, subagents, daily, spend, seenMessages) are views whose get, set, has, delete, clear and entries reach Rust, and a push onto `recentTools` does. Nothing outside live.js changes a field in place but the console's simulate, which uses only what reaches Rust. `sessions` has no set or delete, as nothing sets or forgets a session.

live.js's snapshot and sessionNotes hand out each session's own tokens, context, toolCounts, prompts and messages, which JS holding them sees change (test/golden.test.js relies on it). The twin keeps those as JS objects it writes Rust's state into after every call that changes the session; writing into one doesn't reach Rust. A collisionDiffs list doesn't change with later edits, where JS's was the session's own.

`live.limits` and `live.limitSamples` are { codex, claude } whose fields set Rust's; replacing the whole object, or a sample changed in place, doesn't. `claudeSamples` and `history` are copies, and the activity event emitted is a copy of the history's entry, where JS's were the same objects.

An event keeps a field whose value is undefined (a Codex tool call's agentId). Elsewhere a field JS would hold as undefined is left out (a tool call without a name in the snapshot's lastTool, a Codex subagent without an id, a usage reading that lacks one): the same in JSON.

A count or time a record gives as a string is taken as Number() reads it, where JS's `+` would have joined strings ("5" input tokens). Context used and window keep the value the record gave, as JS did.

A Map key that's an object (a tool_use id that isn't a string, say) matches no other, as a reference does in JS; other keys are told apart as SameValueZero tells them. A value JSON can't hold (NaN, a function) reaches Rust as JSON makes it (NaN as null): only a direct call can pass one.

noteToolResult(ok, ts, tool) from JS doesn't follow `tool`, JS's own copy: Rust keeps its own records of calls. activity(s, ev) for a session that isn't in the map makes it. applyClaudeLine, which took a subagent object JS holds, isn't on the twin (nothing outside live.js calls it). A listener that throws while a line's events are emitted counts the line as an error, after Rust has taken all of it, where JS stopped there.
Sorts by a number (history, subagents, files, resources, Claude samples) are a stable merge sort that counts NaN as equal, as V8's sort does with a comparator that's consistent.

Through the twin, applyClaude takes about 4 times as long as the JS (40,000 lines: 350 ms against 90 ms) and a snapshot about 6 times, since each record crosses into Rust whole and its events come back: a check of the contract, not yet faster.
What stays in JS: the tailer (its own twin), finding the roots (existsSync, realpath), the gatherers of Claude plan usage with their 30-second timer, and the EventEmitter.

Rust decides: the sign-in a credentials text holds, whether it can be used now, the windows an answer gives (parseUsage), why there's no reading (a pause and how long, a refused sign-in, another status, no windows, Anthropic out of reach), when to ask again, and the samples Claude desktop's file holds.

What stays in JS, where the tests hand it in: the keychain read (execFile `security`), the file reads and the path to .credentials.json (node:path, win32 or posix), fetch and res.json(), the vendor schemas' checks (vendor.js's twin), JSON.parse of the desktop file, and the gatherers.
A reset time is read as ISO 8601 (time::parse_iso): one in another format V8's Date.parse takes ("5", "Oct 3 2026") reads as none, where JS read a time. Anthropic sends ISO 8601.
A desktop sample without `t` has no `ts` field, where JS's had one holding undefined.
A signal's `at` reads the line's timestamp as ISO 8601 (time::parse_iso), where V8's Date.parse takes other formats too; both apps write ISO 8601.
The live telemetry's Rust reads every line's signal itself; the twin is for the refusal store and the refusals command.
